html:
The Battle of Sluys was a sea battle fought on 24 June 1340 in the harbour of Sluys, on the coast of Flanders, now Sluis in the Netherlands. The English fleet of King Edward III destroyed a larger French fleet.

The Hundred Years' War had begun three years earlier, when Edward claimed the French crown. France gathered more than 200 ships, some of them hired from Genoa, to stop Edward landing in Flanders and perhaps to invade England. Edward sailed with about 150 ships. The French admirals chained their ships together in three lines across the inlet, like a floating fort. The English came in with the wind and tide behind them. Their longbowmen shot from the ships' castles, and then men-at-arms boarded, ship by ship. Most of the French fleet was captured, and both French commanders died. The French lost perhaps 16,000 to 20,000 men, though the figures are uncertain.

Sluys ended the danger of a French invasion and gave England the upper hand in the Channel for some years. Because of it, the long war was fought on French soil. Edward's army went on to win at Crécy in 1346.
